The Permian Period. Stretching from two hundred and ninety-nine to two hundred and fifty-two million years ago, the Permian saw synapsids rule the land while Pangaea reached its full assembly. It ended catastrophically with the Great Dying—the worst mass extinction in Earth's history, erasing roughly ninety-six percent of marine species and fundamentally reshaping life. The period is named after the Perm region in Russia.

Synapsids, including creatures like Dimetrodon and Therapsids, dominated terrestrial ecosystems, competing with early sauropsid reptiles for ecological niches. The supercontinent Pangaea was fully assembled, creating vast interior deserts and extreme climates, with monsoons raging along the coasts. Reptiles diversified during this period, including the first truly large predators and the ancestors of dinosaurs, the sauropsids.

The Permian extinction struck around two hundred and fifty-two million years ago in what is known as the Great Dying, likely triggered by massive volcanic eruptions in Siberia, ocean anoxia, and climate collapse. Roughly ninety-six percent of marine species and about seventy percent of terrestrial vertebrate families vanished, making it the only extinction that threatened all complex life. The Therapsids, which had dominated the Permian, were nearly wiped out and would cede dominance to reptiles in the Triassic that followed.

The Permian connects directly to the Carboniferous Period before it, when synapsids first rose to dominance, and to the Triassic Period after the extinction, when reptiles inherited the Earth.
